In any case, it cannot be impossible for a lawyer to distinguish the crime of firing the first shot from the crime of being responsible for the war, or still more from the mere preparation of a war.

Nor should it be impossible to recognize the injustice involved in constantly blending those two different offences together—and then blending both of them again with the entirely different crime of inhuman acts, atrocities, and so on.
In relation to the Soviet Union, such distinctions are less than ever mere legal subtleties.

Is it not remarkable that the Hague Regulations on Land Warfare of 1907 are supposed to remain completely unchanged, despite the transformation of political, economic, social, and technical conditions, whenever this works against the defendants;

while at the same time the fundamental concepts underlying those very same Hague Regulations—such as a non-discriminatory concept of war, neutrality, state sovereignty, and the “state” as the sole subject of international law—are completely transformed or abolished whenever this, too, works against the defendants?
Is it a logically fair way of thinking?
But perhaps all of this is thought through far too systematically to be presented in an atmosphere that reacts only impressionistically.
III. On being bound by the “determinations” of the first IMT [International Military Tribunal] judgment:
The purpose is clear: to preserve the foundations of the first trial as a taboo.
To the extent that the first judgment loses the self-evident authority of the reasons on which it was based, the taboo—and this supposed “binding force”—will disappear by itself.
(Dix called my memorandum from the summer of 1945 “a seminar exercise in international law.”)
The point at which the entire logic of objective power relations became choked together with the completely subjective opinions of an individual who happened to possess power.

On the question of whether the word “state” should be used as a universal concept that applies across every historical age, Heinrich Weinstock wrote to me that it was right to resist “turning history into mush.”
“On the other hand, you will probably not succeed in abolishing the word ‘state’ as the now customary name for a ‘political association,’ whatever its structure may be.”
That phrase—“you will probably not succeed”—hit me very hard.

I found it arrogant and irritating. It gives the impression that W. feels entitled to dismiss the whole point of the dispute from some lofty position. He fails to see that we are not dependent on the word “state” in order to have the general term we need.
I never said that general concepts which remove things from their historical setting are impossible or always illegitimate. That would simply be another false generalization.

I say only that such generalizations, though possible, legitimate, and necessary, belong to particular historical periods, and that a word is capable of becoming a valid universal term only within a specific age. For the word “state,” that age is over.
What was the secret—the arcanum—of the word “state”?
With ratio status: reason of state.

All the qualities of the impartial third party—or, in Hegelian language, of objective reason—that were historically connected with the state during this period disappeared once the totality of the state could become an instrument of the totality of a party. And once that happened, the word also lost its logical capacity to serve as a genuine universal concept.
Infinitely important, Gregory the Great, quoted by G. Krauss:

So even Satan’s power, as power, comes from God and is not evil.
How did Burckhardt arrive at the opposite thesis?
The “will to power” would then be the good will!
Yes—provided it is divine power and the will submits itself to it.
There is only one evil will: the will to powerlessness. That is: the refusal to carry out what must be carried out.

The fate of my little essay The Concept of the Political is already becoming part of the concept itself. That is the highest praise one can give the essay.
A sure sign of existential authenticity.

The essay identifies the criterion of the political in the distinction between friend and enemy. And look: the essay itself produces friendship and enmity. It proves that it has the power to arrange whatever encounters it into friends and enemies. It is not studied very much.
Often it is not even read.
Instead it is used, with the greatest intensity, as a criterion.
All of these are good signs.
